summary:
South Sudan's Penal Code criminalises gender presentation on its face. Section 379 reaches "any male person who dresses or is attired in the fashion of a woman", with a penalty of up to three months' imprisonment. The provision requires no sexual conduct and no disclosure of identity, so a trans visitor presenting female is exposed on appearance alone.

The same code treats consensual same-sex sexual conduct as an "unnatural offense", defined as carnal intercourse against the order of nature, punishable by up to 10 years' imprisonment. Where the conduct is nonconsensual, the maximum rises to 14 years.

United States State Department human rights reports for 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022 each record that no authorities were reported to have enforced the same-sex conduct provision. The reports describe no repeal, no moratorium and no prosecutorial policy limiting its use, so non-enforcement is reported practice rather than a legal safeguard.

The same reporting series documents security forces routinely harassing LGBTQI+ people and sometimes arresting, detaining, torturing and beating them between 2018 and 2022. Enforcement pressure falls on people who are visible or suspected rather than on the conduct provision itself.

No hate crime legislation and no anti-discrimination law protect against harassment or abuse on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. A visitor who is targeted has no statutory bias-crime route and no discrimination remedy.

South Sudan recognises no legal status for same-sex couples, and the 2011 Constitution bans same-sex marriage. A trans visitor travelling with a partner in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex holds no recognition and no spousal immigration or next-of-kin standing derived from it.

Stigmatisation of LGBTQ people is widespread in the wider population. The 2011 State Department report described discrimination against gay men and lesbians as "widespread", and the 2022 report found that most openly LGBTQI+ citizens had fled the country because of "actively hostile government rhetoric and action".

No LGBTQ support organisation is known to operate in the country, leaving a visitor who runs into trouble without local advocacy or referral infrastructure.
tangentialFactors:
Official statements have targeted LGBTQ people directly. In September 2017 the minister for Labour, Public Service and Human Resource Development, Gathoth Gatkuoth Hothnyang, said the government would order security forces to arrest LGBTQ persons and detain them until they procreate; no such arrests were reported by the end of that year.

In July 2010 then-President Salva Kiir Mayardit said homosexuality was not in the "character" of Southern Sudanese people and would never gain support. In 2006 bishop Abraham Mayom Athiaan split from the Episcopal Church of Sudan over insufficient condemnation of homosexuality.
localsOnly:
The Non-Governmental Organisations Act (2016) bars organisations from contravening the country's "sovereignty, ... its institutions and laws". Because same-sex activity is illegal, that condition can be used to prevent LGBTQ-supportive civic groups from operating.

Access for All, a community-based LGBTQ-rights group, was intimidated into closing in 2017 after a security force raid; its staff were detained for several months and released without charge, and its executive director later left the country.

Employment protection is limited to one sector. As of 2020, harassment of employees on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited for all oil and gas companies operating in the country. No equivalent rule covers other employers.
outOfScopeNotes:
No entry, visa or passport gender-marker rules specific to trans travellers appear in the source inventory. Airport screening practice and document-marker policy for South Sudan are not sourced here.

Access to gender-affirming care, and the law or practice governing bathrooms and other sex-segregated facilities, is not covered by the inventory.

The enforcement picture rests on State Department reporting that records the absence of reported prosecutions. Absence of reports is not evidence that the conduct provision has never been used, and no sentencing data for either provision is available.

Whether Section 379 has been applied to trans women in practice, and how often, is not documented in the sources reviewed.
